caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant a real petrified man?

No. On 16 October 1869 two men hired to dig a well behind William Newell's barn in Cardiff, New York, uncovered a ten-foot figure of stone. Newell put a tent over it and charged fifty cents for fifteen minutes. Three to five hundred people came a day.

It was made by Newell's cousin, a tobacconist named George Hull, who had lost an argument at a revival meeting about the giants in Genesis. In 1868 he had a 10-foot block of gypsum quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa — the quarrymen were told it was for a Lincoln monument. Chicago sculptors carved it into a copy of Hull himself. Sand, sulphuric acid and steel knitting needles aged the surface and made pores. The whole thing cost him $2,600.

Geologists were not fooled. Yale's Othniel Marsh called it "a most decided humbug": soluble gypsum buried for centuries would not still carry fresh tool marks. Andrew D. White noted there was no reason to dig a well on that spot at all.

Hull sold his interest for $23,000. P. T. Barnum offered $50,000, was refused, and had a plaster copy made instead. Hull confessed on 10 December 1869; both giants were declared fakes in court on 2 February 1870.

Still unresolved: whether the Chicago stonecutter who took the commission knew what he was really carving.

Images: an 1869 lithograph of "The Onondaga Giant" (Popular Graphic Arts); a Bain News Service negative of the giant, 1910; and both sides of an 1873 stereocard of Cardiff Glen, Fort Dodge, Iowa, from the New York Public Library. All public domain.
